You can use modals to express annoyance, criticism, disapproval, promises, threats, preference or reluctance.

Will and would can be used to describe habits or things that are true.
Examples:
Every day, Dan will come to our restaurant and greet all our customers personally.
At school Dan would always follow the teacher's instructions.

You can use will or strong to criticize people's behavior and habits and express annoyance at someone or a situation.
Examples:
The washing machine won't start!
The restaurant is so much quieter without Mike. He would really ruin the atmosphere!

You can use will with an if- clause to suggest disapproval.
Example:
If you will complain so much, I'm not surprised customers are giving you such low ratings!

You use can, could, might or should + infinitive to express criticism or disapproval in the present or in the future.
Examples:
You can be really annoying sometimes!
Our waiters could step up a little more!

You use can, could, might or should + Perfect Infinitive to express criticism or disapproval about a past situation.
Examples:
You could have tried to solve this problem before it became too big. You really should have consulted me on this.

You use Would rather/Would sooner + Simple Past to talk about a preference or strong advice in the present or the future.
Examples:
I'd rather you focused on customer service.
Vanessa would sooner I stayed in the kitchen.

You also use would have preferred to + infinitive to express preference or advice.
Example:
I would have preferred to receive higher ratings.

Modals for Duty and Advice in the Past and Present

You can use a variety of modals to talk about advice, duties and obligations.
You use should, ought to and had better to express advice or strong advice in the present.
You use must to express obligation in the present.
You use should and have to to express duty and obligation in the past.
The most common modals for giving advice are: should, ought toand had better.

Should is the most common modal used to give advice. You also use should for questions.
Ought to is used for giving strong advice.
Had better is much stronger than either should or ought to. It is used to give an order or to suggest that something negative will happen if you refuse the advice.
You cannot use must to express duty or obligation in the past.

You use should + have + Past Participle to express duty in the past.
Example: You should have told me about your problems with the customers yesterday.

You use had to before verbs that talk about necessity. Had to implies that someone else imposed the necessity on you.
Example: You had to leave the kitchen completely clean before you left.

images.text:
Before you interview, you should have prepared the appropriate materials, ideas and guidelines that will result in you making the best choice possible for your team and your restaurant.
  1. Be prepared. You should have looked over the applicant's resume (if attached) and job application so you have at least a cursory idea of the person you're interviewing.
  2. Know what you are looking for. Before interviewing, you ought to know what the position involves and what you expect from the person who fills that position. Managers will have the essential characteristics they're looking for in mind when they hire, and these can help provide a guideline.

1. Ask questions mindfully. When interviewing, you should avoid asking “yes” or “no” questions. These will only get you one word answers. Instead, ask questions that will encourage the applicant to talk about themselves and what makes them distinctive from other applicants. It's important to touch base on their experiences. For example, avoid asking, “Do you have experience as a server?” Instead ask, “What serving experience do you have, and what have you learned from that serving experience?” This is how you will get a feel for the applicant as a person and can see how they can fit into the culture of your staff.

1. Be wary of red flags. Interviews are meant to help you get a feel for the person you might hire. However, sometimes you will begin to see negative signs or red flags in the person's responses. Try to give the applicant the chance to tell you honestly about themselves and their past. However, do not be domineering and do not interject.
  2. Give the applicant time to ask questions. If after several questions you still consider the candidate for the position, give him or her the opportunity to ask questions about the restaurant.
